title: Robotics & Mechatronics
tagline: Robustness over sophistication — making machines move with purpose, where the system is the product.

intro.text: A mechatronic system is not a mechanical system plus an electrical system plus software. It is the set of interactions between them — and every interaction is an interface where an assumption made by one domain meets an assumption made by another.

The bench lie

A robot on a bench with its wheels in the air draws a fraction of its real current, experiences no load torque, has no vibration, and never saturates. Every control gain you tune there is wrong. Every current measurement you take there is meaningless.

Tune under load, on the surface you will actually drive on, with the battery you will actually use, at the state of charge it will actually be at. The number of student robots that work perfectly in the lab and fail in the corridor is not a coincidence — it is a measurement methodology problem.

modules.title: Choosing Parts That Exist in India

intro.text: The best component is the one that meets your derated requirement and is on a shelf you can reach this week. A marginally better part with a three-week import lead time has, for a one-semester project, infinite cost.

topics.title: Requirement → specification → candidate → verification

blocks.text: 1 Requirement is physical and comes from your system: ‘must climb a 10° ramp carrying 2 kg at 0.4 m/s’. 2 Specification is the derated number you shop with: compute what you need, then apply the margins in §2.2. Shopping

with an underated requirement is how you buy a motor that works until the first ramp. 3 Candidates are parts that exist, in India, at a price you can pay. Two or three, not one — the first choice will be out of
stock. 4 Verification is measuring the part you received. Hobby-grade specifications are optimistic and counterfeits are
common. Measure the stall current, weigh the part, time the servo, load-test the battery.
Hobby specifications are marketing, not datasheets

Assume, until you have measured otherwise: battery capacity is 50–70% of the printed mAh; servo torque is at the stated voltage only and falls off sharply below it; motor RPM is at no load and drops by a third or more under working load; ‘±2 cm’ sensor accuracy is at the ideal target, ideal reflectivity and ideal temperature. None of this is unusual — it is simply what unbranded hobby parts are. Design with margin and measure what you receive.

topics.title: Motor drivers — where beginners lose the most performance

blocks.text: Stop using the L298N It is the module everyone starts with and it is a bipolar-transistor design from 1988. It drops roughly 2 V across the output stage, which at 6 V motor supply means a third of your battery is heating the driver rather than turning the wheel. It also runs hot, needs a heatsink, and its current rating is optimistic. Use a MOSFET driver instead. A TB6612FNG (about ₹150–300, ~1.2 A per channel continuous) drops a fraction of a volt and is a straight swap for small robots. For larger motors, a BTS7960 module or a Cytron MDD10A handles far more current cleanly. Your battery life and your low-speed control will both improve immediately, and low-speed control is exactly what a line follower needs.

blocks.text: BATTERY Li-ion 18650 pack (3S = 11.1 V nominal) with a BMS, or a LiPo with a low-voltage alarm. Never run cells below cut-off. Capacity: size for 2x your target runtime.

battery ──┬── FUSE ── E-STOP ──── motor driver (raw pack V) │ ├── buck ── 5.0 V ── MCU, sensors │ └── buck ── 6.0 V ── servos (own bulk cap)

intro.text: Textbook PID assumes a linear plant, continuous time, unlimited actuator authority and clean measurement. Your robot has none of these. Everything in this chapter is about the gap between those two situations.

topics.title: When you do not need a control loop

blocks.text: Open loop is not a lesser choice. If the disturbance is small and the consequence of error is small, a calibrated open-loop command is simpler, cheaper and has no gains to tune. A servo commanded to 90° is open loop from your side. A line follower driving straight on flat ground barely needs a loop at all.

Close the loop when the disturbance is significant and unpredictable — a gradient, a varying payload, battery voltage sagging over a run, one motor being 20% weaker than its twin. That last one is why two ‘identical’ hobby motors do not drive a robot straight, and it is the most common first reason to add encoders.

topics.title: A PID that survives contact with hardware

blocks.text: // Discrete PID for real actuators. Fixed dt, anti-windup, filtered // derivative on measurement, output clamping, deadband feedforward.
struct PID {
float kp, ki, kd;
float outMin, outMax; // actuator limits, in the units you command
float tau; // derivative low-pass time constant, seconds
float deadband; // measured minimum effective command (3.4)
// state
float integral, dFilt, prevMeasurement;
bool first;
static float clampf(float v, float lo, float hi) { return v < lo ? lo : (v > hi ? hi : v);
float pid_update(PID *p, float setpoint, float measurement, float dt) { float error = setpoint - measurement;
// ---- P float P = p->kp * error;

// ---- D on MEASUREMENT, not on error. // Differentiating the error makes the output spike every time the // setpoint changes ("derivative kick"). Differentiating the measurement // gives the same damping with no kick. if (p->first) { p->prevMeasurement = measurement; p->dFilt = 0; p->first = false; } float rawD = -(measurement - p->prevMeasurement) / dt; // first-order low-pass: raw encoder derivative is far too noisy to use float alpha = dt / (p->tau + dt); p->dFilt += alpha * (rawD - p->dFilt); float D = p->kd * p->dFilt;
// ---- I with conditional integration (anti-windup) float unsat = P + p->integral + D; bool windingUp = (unsat > p->outMax && error > 0.0f) ||
(unsat < p->outMin && error < 0.0f); if (!windingUp) {
p->integral += p->ki * error * dt; p->integral = clampf(p->integral, p->outMin, p->outMax); }
// ---- combine and clamp float out = clampf(P + p->integral + D, p->outMin, p->outMax);
// ---- deadband feedforward: push past static friction so that a small
// error produces a command the motor can actually act on.
if (out > 0.5f) out += p->deadband;
else if (out < -0.5f) out -= p->deadband;
else out = 0.0f; // genuinely zero: let it rest
out = clampf(out, p->outMin, p->outMax);
p->prevMeasurement = measurement; return out; }
Four things here that the textbook version omits and that matter more than the gains: derivative on measurement, filtered derivative, conditional-integration anti-windup, and deadband feedforward
Fixed dt is not a detail

Call your control loop at a fixed rate and pass the real elapsed time, not a constant you hoped was true. If your loop runs at 100 Hz sometimes and 60 Hz when the telemetry sends, your effective Ki and Kd change from cycle to cycle and no amount of tuning will make the robot behave consistently.

Structure it as a timed loop: check micros(), run when the interval has elapsed, and measure your actual jitter once. Never put delay(), a blocking ultrasonic read, or a serial print of more than a few bytes inside the control path.

topics.title: Measure your deadband before you tune anything

blocks.text: PROCEDURE - 15 minutes, and it changes your low-speed behaviour completely
1. Put the robot ON THE GROUND, loaded as it will really be. Not on blocks. Friction with the wheels in the air is a different number.
2. Command PWM = 0. Increase by 1 every 300 ms, printing the command and the encoder count.

3. Record the command at which the wheel FIRST moves. -> break-away Then reduce slowly and record where it STOPS moving. -> keep-moving Break-away is always higher. The difference is your static friction.
4. Repeat for reverse, and for the other motor. They will differ, often by 10-20%. Store one deadband value per motor per direction.
TYPICAL RESULT on a small geared robot with an 8-bit PWM range:
break-away ~ 55 / 255 keep-moving ~ 35 / 255
Meaning: roughly the bottom fifth of your control range does nothing.
Without feedforward, every small correction your PID makes is discarded
by the hardware, and the integrator has to wind up to compensate.
USE keep-moving as the deadband feedforward value, not break-away - using break-away makes the robot jump on every direction reversal.
Do this on every motor, on the real surface, with the real battery at mid charge. Write the four numbers into your code as named constants

topics.title: A tuning procedure that works on a robot

blocks.text: 1 Fix the mechanics first. If there is visible slop, a loose grub screw or a wheel that wobbles, no gain will help. Tuning is the last step, not the first.
2 Verify the loop rate and the sign of your feedback. A sign error looks exactly like instability and wastes hours. Command a small positive output and confirm the measurement increases.
3 Set the deadband feedforward from §3.4. Now a small command produces small motion, which is what the rest of the tuning assumes.
4 Kp only. Ki = Kd = 0. Raise Kp until the response oscillates steadily, then halve it. You are looking for brisk response with a small overshoot.

5 Add Kd to damp the overshoot. Increase until the motion becomes rough or buzzy, then back off by a third. If the buzz appears immediately, increase the derivative filter time constant tau — you are amplifying encoder noise, not damping motion.

6 Add Ki last, and sparingly. Only enough to remove the steady-state error you actually care about. Most mobile-robot loops need far less Ki than people give them; an aggressive integrator on a system with backlash produces a permanent hunt.

7 Re-test under the conditions that matter: fully loaded, on the real surface, on a gradient, and with the battery at 30% charge. Gains tuned at full charge will be sluggish at the end of a run because your effective actuator authority has dropped.
Ziegler–Nichols is a starting point, not an answer

The classical tuning rules assume a plant that your robot is not. They will get you into the right order of magnitude and they will overshoot badly on a system with backlash. Use them to find a starting Kp, then tune by observation — and log the step response so you are comparing plots rather than impressions. A phone video of the robot is a legitimate measurement instrument at this stage.

topics.title: Feedforward: do the predictable part without the loop

blocks.text: The feedback loop should correct errors, not do the whole job. If you already know roughly what command produces a given speed, apply it directly and let PID handle only the difference. This reduces the gain you need, which reduces every problem in §3.2.
// Measure this once: command 20%, 40%, 60%, 80% PWM and record steady
// speed at each. Fit a straight line. That IS your feedforward model.
// command = Kff * targetSpeed + deadband (per direction)
float ff = KFF * targetSpeed; float fb = pid_update(&velPid, targetSpeed, measuredSpeed, dt); float cmd = clampf(ff + fb, -255, 255);
// With a decent feedforward, the PID output stays small and the loop // becomes far more forgiving. If your PID is doing 90% of the work, // you have not characterised your actuator yet.
This is the single highest-value technique in the chapter and the one most often skipped in student code

topics.title: Backlash: design around it, do not control through it

blocks.text: Backlash is free play — the gearbox output does not move for the first few degrees after a direction reversal. To the controller this looks like the plant briefly having zero gain, and the standard reaction — more gain — produces a limit cycle: the joint buzzes back and forth across the dead zone forever.
• Measure it. Hold the output, rotate the input by hand, and record how far it moves before the output responds. On a hobby servo it is commonly 1–3°; on a cheap spur gearbox it can be much more.

• Approach from one direction. For positioning tasks, always overshoot the target slightly and come back the same way every time. This converts backlash from an error into a constant offset you can calibrate out — the standard trick in machine tools and the reason Project 2 uses it.

• Reduce it mechanically. Preloaded gears, a belt instead of a gear train, sensing at the output rather than the motor shaft. Belts have compliance but almost no backlash, which is usually the better trade for a student arm.
• Accept a dead zone in the specification. If you have 2° of backlash, do not promise 0.5° repeatability. Write the achievable number down and design the task so it does not need more.

BUILD THIS — Tune one motor properly Two hours on a single motor. Everything in Chapters 4–6 depends on this. 1 Wire one motor with an encoder. Confirm the encoder counts up when the motor drives forward. 2 Build the timed loop at 100 Hz and print actual loop interval. Confirm the jitter is small before continuing. 3 Run the deadband procedure in §3.4. Record four numbers. 4 Build the feedforward line from §3.6 by measuring speed at four PWM values. 5 Tune Kp, then Kd, then Ki using §3.5. Log a step response at each stage and keep the plots — they are your evidence and
your report. 6 Now repeat the step test with 2 kg on the robot and the battery half flat. Note how much worse it is. That gap is what
Chapter 7 is about.

topics.title: The sunlight problem, and the fix that makes this project work

blocks.text: An IR reflectance sensor measures how much infrared its phototransistor sees. Indoors, that is almost entirely the light from its own LED bouncing off the floor. Outdoors it is mostly sunlight, which contains far more infrared than your LED emits. In direct sun the reading saturates and the sensor is effectively blind — which is why a robot that worked all week in the lab fails in the first patch of daylight.

Differential (chopped) measurement — do this and the problem disappears Instead of reading the sensor once, read it twice: once with your IR LED off, and once with it on. Subtract. The ambient contribution appears in both readings and cancels; what remains is only your own LED’s reflected light.
reflectance = read(LED on) − read(LED off)

The two readings must be close together in time — a few hundred microseconds — so the ambient level has not changed between them. This costs you one extra ADC conversion and one GPIO pin to switch the LED bank, and it converts a sensor that fails outdoors into one that works. It is the single most important technique in this chapter.
// Ambient-cancelling read. LED bank on a GPIO, sensors on ADC pins. // Works with discrete TCRT5000s or a QTR array wired for controlled emitters.
const uint8_t SENS[N] = {32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 39}; // ESP32 ADC pins const uint8_t LED_BANK = 25;
void readLine(uint16_t out[N]) { static uint16_t dark[N];
digitalWrite(LED_BANK, LOW); // ---- ambient only
delayMicroseconds(200); // let the phototransistor settle
for (uint8_t i = 0; i < N; i++) dark[i] = analogRead(SENS[i]);
digitalWrite(LED_BANK, HIGH); // ---- ambient + our LED
delayMicroseconds(200);
for (uint8_t i = 0; i < N; i++) {
int v = (int)analogRead(SENS[i]) - (int)dark[i];
out[i] = v > 0 ? v : 0; // negative means ambient changed; treat as 0
digitalWrite(LED_BANK, LOW); // LEDs off between reads: saves power,
} // reduces heating and drift

// CALIBRATION - run once at the start of every deployment, on the actual // surface, in the actual light. Sweep the robot across the line by hand // for ~5 seconds while recording min/max per sensor, then normalise: // // norm[i] = 1000 * (raw[i] - min[i]) / max(1, (max[i] - min[i])) // // Normalising per sensor is what makes six mismatched hobby sensors and // a sensor bar that is not perfectly parallel to the ground behave alike.
Recalibrate every time the light or surface changes. A calibration from yesterday indoors is not valid today outdoors, and this is a 5-second operation

topics.title: Mechanical design for uneven ground

blocks.text: • Sensor height is the critical dimension. Reflectance falls off sharply with distance. On a flat floor you would mount at 5 mm; over paver blocks with 8 mm steps, a rigid 5 mm mount will strike the ground. Mount at 10–12 mm and accept lower signal, or make the mount compliant.

• Make the sensor bar compliant, not rigid. Mount it on a small sprung or rubber-isolated arm with a skid, so it follows the surface while the chassis rides over steps. This is a mechanical solution to what looks like a sensor problem, which is the theme of this whole guide.

• Put the sensor bar ahead of the wheels — typically 60–100 mm. This gives the controller preview: it sees the curve before the robot reaches it. Too far forward and the geometry becomes unstable on tight turns.
• Wheelbase and track. A short wheelbase turns tightly but wanders; a long one is stable but cuts corners. Start with track ≈ wheelbase and adjust after testing on the real path.
• Ground clearance elsewhere. Everything except the sensor skid should clear the worst step by 2×. A robot that high-centres on a paver edge is not a control problem.
• Castor or ball wheel at the back — a ball castor jams in paver joints. A larger-diameter castor wheel, or a third driven wheel, rolls over gaps that a small ball drops into.

topics.title: From sensors to a line position

blocks.text: // Weighted average gives a CONTINUOUS position estimate from a handful of // discrete sensors - far better than "which sensor is darkest". // Positions in thousandths: sensor i sits at 1000*i.
int32_t linePosition(const uint16_t norm[N], bool *seen) {
uint32_t weighted = 0, total = 0;
for (uint8_t i = 0; i < N; i++) {
if (norm[i] > 200) { // noise floor, tune on real data
weighted += (uint32_t)norm[i] * (i * 1000);
total += norm[i];
*seen = (total > 0);
if (!*seen) return 0;
return (int32_t)(weighted / total); // 0 .. (N-1)*1000
// error, centred on zero: // int32_t centre = (N - 1) * 1000 / 2; // int32_t error = pos - centre;
// SPEED SCHEDULING - the difference between a demo and something that
// survives a real path. Slow down when the line is curving or uncertain.
// float curvature = fabs(error) / (float)centre; // 0 .. 1
// float speed = BASE_SPEED * (1.0f - 0.65f * curvature);
// A constant-speed line follower will leave the line at the first sharp
// bend. This one line of code fixes most of that.
Weighted-average position plus curvature-based speed scheduling is most of what separates a robot that finishes the path from one that does not

topics.title: Behaviour: what happens when the line is gone

blocks.text: On a campus path the line will be lost — a puddle, a patch of mud, a repaired section, a shadow edge, a gap in the paint. A follower with no recovery behaviour drives off into the grass. Make the behaviour explicit as a state machine.
line seen

│ error │ │ │ │ known │
│ all sensors dark │ found
│ (intersection / thick line) │▲

the robot panics several times per metre.

topics.title: The control loop, assembled

blocks.text: // Fixed-rate loop. Nothing here blocks. This is the whole robot.

const uint32_t LOOP_US = 10000;       // 100 Hz
uint32_t nextLoop = 0;

void loop() { uint32_t now = micros(); if ((int32_t)(now - nextLoop) < 0) return; // not yet - do other work float dt = (now - nextLoop + LOOP_US) / 1e6f; nextLoop += LOOP_US; if ((int32_t)(micros() - nextLoop) > 0) nextLoop = micros() + LOOP_US; // catch up
// ---- SENSE
uint16_t norm[N];
readLine(norm); // ambient-cancelled (4.2)
bool seen;
int32_t pos = linePosition(norm, &seen);
int32_t centre = (N - 1) * 1000 / 2;
float error = (float)(pos - centre);
// ---- DECIDE (state machine from figure 4.1) state = updateState(seen, allDark(norm), dt);
float steer = 0.0f, base = 0.0f;
switch (state) {
case FOLLOW: {
steer = pid_update(&linePid, 0.0f, error, dt); // drive error to 0
float curvature = fabsf(error) / (float)centre; // 0 .. 1
base = BASE_SPEED * (1.0f - 0.65f * curvature); // slow in the bends
lastSteer = steer;
break;
case COAST: // brief dropout: hold course
steer = lastSteer * 0.7f; base = BASE_SPEED * 0.5f; break;
case SEARCH: // arc toward last known side
steer = copysignf(SEARCH_STEER, lastSteer); base = SEARCH_SPEED; break;
case INTERSECTION:
steer = 0.0f; base = BASE_SPEED * 0.6f; break;
case STOPPED:
steer = 0.0f; base = 0.0f; break;

// ---- ACT: differential mixing, then clamp TOGETHER so that clipping // one wheel does not silently change the commanded curvature. float l = base - steer, r = base + steer; float peak = fmaxf(fabsf(l), fabsf(r)); if (peak > PWM_MAX) { l *= PWM_MAX / peak; r *= PWM_MAX / peak; } setMotor(LEFT, l); setMotor(RIGHT, r); }

// Why scale both wheels instead of clamping each: clamping the outer wheel // alone reduces the turn rate exactly when the robot most needs it, and the // robot understeers out of every sharp corner. Scaling preserves the ratio.
PROTOCOL — Test protocol — Project 1
Run these in order. Do not skip to stage 5 because the robot looks ready.
STAGE 1 BENCH, wheels up - sensor read plausible? print all N normalised values - move a black card under each sensor, confirm it responds - confirm ambient cancellation: shine a phone torch on the

- lay 5 mm strips across the path every 200 mm - does the sensor bar stay in range? does COAST trigger
correctly, or does it drop to SEARCH on every strip?
STAGE 4 OUTDOOR, SHADE, real pavers - recalibrate first. Run 20 m. Count interventions. - log: interventions per 10 m. This is your headline metric.
- recalibrate. Run the same 20 m. - if interventions rise sharply vs stage 4, the ambient
cancellation or the calibration is the cause, not the PID.
- wet pavers are specular: they reflect the LED away from the sensor. Expect degradation. Record it rather than hiding it.

intro.text: Almost every first robot arm sags, jitters, browns out the controller, or cannot lift what it was built for. All four have the same root cause: the torque budget was never calculated. Ten minutes of arithmetic before you order parts prevents all of it.

topics.title: Specification

blocks.text: REACH 300 mm from shoulder axis, in a horizontal plane
PAYLOAD 100 g at full reach (a small component, a connector, a bolt)
REPEATABILITY +/- 3 mm at the gripper, returning to the same point
from the SAME direction (see 5.5 - direction matters)
CYCLE pick and place within a 400 x 300 mm work area, 8 s/cycle
DOF 4: base rotation, shoulder, elbow, gripper
BUDGET Rs 4,000 - 7,000
absolute accuracy (we have no joint feedback - 5.2) smooth Cartesian straight-line motion anything above 150 g, ever
Repeatability and accuracy are different things. With hobby servos you can achieve useful repeatability and almost no accuracy — design the task around that

topics.title: What a hobby servo actually is

blocks.text: A hobby servo is a small DC motor, a plastic or metal gearbox, a potentiometer and a closed-loop controller in a box. You send it a pulse width; it tries to reach the corresponding position. Five consequences that shape the whole design:

• You get no feedback. You command a position; you never learn whether it arrived, stalled, or was pushed aside. Your software is flying blind, which is why §5.6 uses timed, verified motions rather than assuming success.

• Torque is specified at a specific voltage and falls off below it. An MG996R rated around 11 kg·cm at 6 V delivers noticeably less at 5 V, and much less when hot after a few minutes of holding a load.
• Holding costs current. A servo resisting a load draws current continuously even when nothing moves. An arm holding a payload at full extension is a sustained electrical load, not a static one.

• Stall current is large and sudden. A standard servo can pull well over an amp when it hits an end stop or a jam. Four servos doing this at once is what browns out the microcontroller and resets your program mid-cycle.
• They jitter. Cheap servos hunt around the commanded position, especially under load and especially on a noisy supply. Some of this is the servo; a lot of it is your power rail.

Never power servos from the controller board Not from the Arduino 5 V pin, not from the ESP32 regulator, not from USB. The board regulator cannot supply servo current and the resulting rail collapse resets your MCU at exactly the moment the arm is moving. The correct arrangement: a separate buck converter sized for total stall current, feeding the servos directly; a 1000 µF electrolytic capacitor across the servo rail physically close to the servos; and the servo ground tied to the MCU ground at one point. Signal wires carry only the pulse. This single change fixes most ‘my arm behaves randomly’ problems.

blocks.text: Servo torque is quoted in kg·cm: the mass in kilograms it can hold at one centimetre from the shaft. A load of m kilograms at L centimetres needs m × L kg·cm. Every mass on the arm contributes, at its own distance, and the worst case is the arm fully extended and horizontal.

topics.title: Inverse kinematics for a two-link planar arm

blocks.text: Given a target point, find the joint angles. For two links in a plane there is a closed-form solution — no iteration, no library, about fifteen lines.
#include <math.h>

// Returns false if (x, y) is outside the workspace. Angles in radians: // th1 measured from +X axis at the shoulder, th2 is the elbow angle // relative to link 1. elbowUp selects between the two valid solutions. bool ik2(float x, float y, float L1, float L2, bool elbowUp,
float *th1, float *th2) { float r2 = x * x + y * y; float r = sqrtf(r2);

// Reachability: annulus between |L1-L2| and L1+L2. // Check this BEFORE the trig, and keep a margin off the outer edge - // near full extension the arm loses all vertical stiffness. if (r > (L1 + L2) * 0.98f || r < fabsf(L1 - L2) * 1.02f) return false;
if (c2 < -1.0f) c2 = -1.0f; // guard against rounding
float s2 = sqrtf(1.0f - c2 * c2);
if (!elbowUp) s2 = -s2;
*th2 = atan2f(s2, c2); *th1 = atan2f(y, x) - atan2f(L2 * s2, L1 + L2 * c2); return true; }
// Mapping joint angle to a servo pulse. Every servo differs; calibrate
// each one and store its own constants. Never assume 500-2500 us = 0-180.
uint16_t angleToUs(float rad, const ServoCal *c) {
float deg = rad * 57.2957795f;
deg = deg * c->direction + c->offsetDeg; // direction = +1 or -1
if (deg < c->minDeg) deg = c->minDeg; // software end stops:
if (deg > c->maxDeg) deg = c->maxDeg; // protect the mechanism
return (uint16_t)(c->usAtZero + deg * c->usPerDeg);
The reachability check with a 2% margin matters: commanding a point at exactly full extension gives a singular, floppy configuration and the servos fight each other

topics.title: Calibration, backlash and repeatability

blocks.text: • Calibrate each servo individually. Command a few known pulse widths, measure the actual angle with a printed protractor, and fit usPerDeg and usAtZero. Two servos from the same batch will differ by several degrees.
• Measure your link lengths after assembly, not from the CAD. A 3 mm error in L1 becomes several millimetres of position error at the gripper.

• Always approach a target from the same direction (§3.7). Overshoot by 5° and come back. This converts gearbox backlash from a random error into a constant offset your calibration absorbs, and it is the single biggest improvement to repeatability you can make in software.
• Let the arm settle. Command the move, then wait — typically 200–400 ms — before closing the gripper. Servos have no ‘arrived’ signal, so the delay is your arrival check.
• Move joints in the right order. Lift, traverse, then lower. Moving all joints simultaneously toward a target sweeps the gripper along an unpredictable arc that will collide with the workpiece.

topics.title: Sequencing without delay()

blocks.text: The instinctive way to write a pick-and-place cycle is a chain of servo.write() and delay() calls. It works on the bench and it is unusable in a real system: while the arm is delaying, nothing can read a sensor, respond to an e-stop, or notice that the cycle has jammed. Use a state machine with interpolated motion instead.

// Interpolated, non-blocking joint motion. Servos jump to a commanded // position at full speed, which shakes the arm and overshoots. Ramping the // command over time gives smooth motion and much better repeatability.
typedef struct { float from, to, t, dur; bool active; } Move; Move mv[NJOINTS];
void startMove(int j, float target, float seconds) { mv[j].from = jointAngle[j]; mv[j].to = target; mv[j].t = 0; mv[j].dur = seconds; mv[j].active = true;
bool movesDone(void) { for (int j = 0; j < NJOINTS; j++) if (mv[j].active) return false; return true;

void updateMoves(float dt) { for (int j = 0; j < NJOINTS; j++) { if (!mv[j].active) continue; mv[j].t += dt; float u = mv[j].t / mv[j].dur; if (u >= 1.0f) { u = 1.0f; mv[j].active = false; } // smoothstep: zero velocity at both ends, no jerk at start or stop float s = u * u * (3.0f - 2.0f * u); jointAngle[j] = mv[j].from + s * (mv[j].to - mv[j].from); writeServo(j, angleToUs(jointAngle[j], &cal[j])); }
// ---- the cycle, as a state machine. Called every loop, never blocks. enum { S_IDLE, S_ABOVE_PICK, S_DOWN, S_GRIP, S_LIFT, S_ABOVE_PLACE,
void cycleStep(float dt) {
updateMoves(dt);
if (!movesDone()) { // still moving: check for a jam
if ((millis() - stateEntered) > STATE_TIMEOUT_MS) { state = S_FAULT; }
return;
if (settleRemaining > 0) { settleRemaining -= dt; return; } // let it settle
switch (state) {
case S_ABOVE_PICK:
// approach every target from the SAME direction (3.7, 5.5): come in
// from above and from +X, always. Backlash becomes a constant offset.
moveToXY(pick.x + APPROACH_MM, pick.y, HOVER_Z, 0.8f);
next(S_DOWN, 0.20f); break;
case S_DOWN: moveToXY(pick.x, pick.y, pick.z, 0.6f); next(S_GRIP, 0.30f); break;
case S_GRIP: gripper(CLOSED); next(S_LIFT, 0.40f); break;
case S_LIFT: moveToXY(pick.x, pick.y, HOVER_Z, 0.5f);
next(S_ABOVE_PLACE, 0.10f); break;
// ... place mirrors pick ...
case S_FAULT: relaxAllServos(); alarm(); break; // never leave a
} // servo stalled

The S_FAULT path matters: a servo held against a jam draws stall current continuously and will strip its gears or burn out within minutes. A timeout that relaxes the servos is the cheapest insurance in the project
PROTOCOL — Test protocol — Project 2

STAGE 1  POWER, before any mechanics
         - servo rail under load: command all servos to move together
while watching the rail with a meter. It must stay within about 0.3 V of nominal. If it dips, your supply or your capacitor is inadequate. Fix this first; everything else downstream depends on it.
- calibrate each servo (5.5), record its constants - sweep each joint to its software end stops, slowly, and
confirm nothing collides or over-travels
- command a 100 mm square path at slow speed - mark the four corners on paper under the gripper - measure the error at each corner. This is your accuracy.
Expect several millimetres. That is normal and acceptable.

STAGE 4  REPEATABILITY - the number that actually matters
         - command the SAME point 20 times, always approached from
the same direction, returning to home in between - mark each attempt on paper. Measure the spread. - PASS: spread within +/- 3 mm. - Then repeat approaching from the OPPOSITE direction and
measure again. The difference between the two clusters is your backlash, in millimetres, at the gripper.
- repeat stage 4 holding 100 g. Repeatability will worsen.
Record by how much. - run 30 continuous cycles. Touch the shoulder servo
afterwards: if it is too hot to hold, it is undersized, regardless of what stage 4 said.
- block the gripper mid-cycle. Does anything strip, or does
the software notice and stop? Add a cycle timeout. - cut power mid-cycle. Does the arm fall onto the work area?
If so, add a mechanical rest position.
Stage 5’s heat check catches undersized servos that pass every positional test. A servo that is hot after thirty cycles will fail in the fourth week.

intro.text: The interesting question is not whether you can afford a LiDAR. It is whether metric SLAM is the right architecture for a bot that runs the same three routes across a campus every day. For that problem it is usually not — and the alternative is cheaper, more robust and far easier to debug.

topics.title: An honest word about LiDAR

blocks.text: Cheap 2D LiDAR exists now. It is still the wrong choice here.

Entry-level 2D LiDAR has fallen dramatically — driven largely by robot vacuum cleaners — and units in the roughly ₹5,000–₹9,000 range are now common, with salvaged vacuum-cleaner units cheaper still. So ‘too expensive’ is no longer the honest objection. Three better ones:

Sunlight. Entry 2D LiDARs are commonly rated for ambient light around 2 klux — an indoor figure. Direct Indian sunlight is well over 100 klux. Units specified to work in strong sun (40–80 klux) exist and cost several times more. An outdoor campus bot with a ₹6,000 indoor LiDAR is carrying a sensor that goes blind at 11 a.m.

Compute and complexity. SLAM needs a Linux-class board, a working ROS 2 stack, and real tuning effort. That is a semester in itself, and it is a different semester from the one where you learn integration.
Architecture. SLAM builds a map so a robot can localise anywhere. Your bot runs fixed routes between known points. Building a full metric map to solve that is like using GPS to find your own kitchen.

topics.title: Topological navigation — the right architecture for this problem

blocks.text: METRIC SLAM TOPOLOGICAL (what we build)

builds a centimetre-accurate map       stores a GRAPH of known places
localises anywhere in it               travels between adjacent nodes
needs LiDAR/vision + heavy compute     needs odometry + heading + a
fails confusingly when it fails        few cheap range sensors
                                       fails obviously and safely
└───┘ "corridor, wall on └───┘ "ramp up 5°" └───┘
lab right, ends at door" lift office
Each EDGE carries: distance, heading, and a TERMINATION CONDITION -
the thing that says "you have arrived", independent of odometry:
"front ToF reads < 400 mm" (a wall)
"right ToF steps from <500 to >1500 mm" (a doorway edge)
"line sensor sees the floor marker"
"bump switch closes"

The termination condition is what stops odometry drift accumulating across the whole route. Every node arrival RESETS the position estimate. Drift now only has to survive ONE edge, not the entire journey.
Figure 6.1 — This is the key idea in the chapter. Odometry is unreliable over 100 m and perfectly adequate over 12 m if something external tells you when you have arrived.

topics.title: Odometry and heading

blocks.text: // Differential-drive odometry. Call at a fixed rate from the control loop. // Units: metres and radians. Wheel radius R, wheelbase W (wheel centre to // wheel centre), CPR = encoder counts per wheel revolution AFTER gearing.
void odomUpdate(long dLeftTicks, long dRightTicks, Pose *p) { float dL = 2.0f * M_PI * R * (float)dLeftTicks / (float)CPR; float dR = 2.0f * M_PI * R * (float)dRightTicks / (float)CPR;
float dC = 0.5f * (dL + dR); // centre travel // heading change float dTheta = (dR - dL) / W;
// Midpoint integration: use the average heading over the step. Plain
// Euler (using the old heading) accumulates noticeable error on curves.
p->x += dC * cosf(p->theta + 0.5f * dTheta);
p->y += dC * sinf(p->theta + 0.5f * dTheta);
p->theta = wrapPi(p->theta + dTheta);
// HEADING FUSION - odometry heading drifts because of wheel slip and
// because W is never exactly what you measured. Gyro heading drifts
// because of bias. They drift for DIFFERENT reasons, so fuse them.
// gyro: good over seconds, drifts over minutes
// odometry: good on average, wrong whenever a wheel slips
void headingUpdate(float gyroZ, float odomDTheta, float dt, float *theta) {
static float bias = 0.0f;
// Estimate gyro bias while genuinely stationary - do this on every stop.
if (isStationary()) bias += 0.001f * (gyroZ - bias);
float gyroDelta = (gyroZ - bias) * dt;
const float A = 0.98f; // trust the gyro short-term
*theta = wrapPi(*theta + A * gyroDelta + (1.0f - A) * odomDTheta);

// Do NOT use a magnetometer for heading on a robot with motors on it. // The magnetic field near a running DC motor swamps the earth's field, // and every steel door frame on campus shifts it further.
Re-estimate the gyro bias every time the robot stops. Bias drifts with temperature, and on a 30-minute run in the sun the temperature changes a lot

Because edges are short and each node arrival resets the estimate, none of these accumulate across a route. That is the entire argument for topological navigation on a budget.

topics.title: Behaviour arbitration and the safety layer

blocks.text: // Fixed priority. The highest-priority behaviour that WANTS control, // gets it. Simple, deterministic, and trivial to debug - you can always // print which behaviour is driving.
typedef enum { B_ESTOP, B_CLIFF, B_BUMP, B_AVOID, B_NAV, B_IDLE } Behaviour;
Behaviour arbitrate(const Sensors *s) {
if (s->estopOpen) return B_ESTOP; // hardware also cuts
if (s->cliffFront > CLIFF_MM) return B_CLIFF; // downward ToF: a step
if (s->bumpLeft || s->bumpRight) return B_BUMP; // physical contact
if (s->frontRange < AVOID_MM) return B_AVOID;
if (navHasGoal()) return B_NAV;
return B_IDLE;
// It clamps whatever the behaviours asked for. void safetyClamp(float *v, float *w, const Sensors *s) {

// 1. speed limited by forward clearance - always able to stop in the // distance you can see float vMax = (s->frontRange - STOP_MARGIN_MM) / 1000.0f * K_STOP; if (vMax < 0) vMax = 0; if (*v > vMax) *v = vMax;
// 2. hard ceiling. A delivery bot among people has no business // exceeding walking pace. if (*v > V_MAX) *v = V_MAX;
// 3. watchdog: if the high-level planner has not spoken recently, // it has crashed. Stop. if (millis() - lastNavUpdate > 500) { *v = 0; *w = 0; }
// 4. tilt: if the IMU says we are on an unexpected slope or falling // over, stop and alarm. if (fabsf(s->pitch) > TILT_LIMIT || fabsf(s->roll) > TILT_LIMIT) {
The safety clamp must live on the microcontroller, not on the Linux board. If Linux hangs, the MCU still stops the robot — that is the whole reason for the two-brain architecture in §2.3

topics.title: Executing one edge

blocks.text: // One edge of the graph: drive a heading for a distance, until the // termination condition fires. Odometry provides steering; the termination // condition provides truth. This function is the heart of the navigator.

typedef struct {              // desired heading, radians
   float heading;             // expected length, metres (a sanity bound)
   float distance;            // TERM_FRONT_WALL, TERM_RIGHT_OPENING, ...
   uint8_t termType;          // e.g. 0.40 m
   float termParam;
} Edge;

EdgeResult runEdge(const Edge *e, const Sensors *s, Pose *p, float dt) { // --- heading hold: a small PID on heading error, NOT on position. // Trying to servo to an (x, y) target amplifies odometry error; // holding a heading and letting the termination condition decide // arrival is far more robust with cheap sensors. float hErr = wrapPi(e->heading - p->theta); float w = pid_update(&headingPid, 0.0f, -hErr, dt); float v = V_CRUISE;
// --- slow down near the expected end so termination is not overshot float travelled = distanceSince(edgeStartPose, *p); if (travelled > e->distance * 0.80f) v *= 0.5f;
// --- termination: the external check that resets accumulated drift
bool arrived = false;
switch (e->termType) {
case TERM_FRONT_WALL:
arrived = (s->frontRange < e->termParam); break;
case TERM_RIGHT_OPENING: // wall ends -> doorway
arrived = (prevRight < 0.5f && s->rightRange > 1.5f); break;
case TERM_MARKER:
arrived = markerSeen(e->termParam); break;
case TERM_DISTANCE_ONLY: // last resort - drifts
arrived = (travelled >= e->distance); break;

// --- overshoot guard: if we have gone 30% past the expected length and // the condition has not fired, something is wrong. Stop rather than // continue into unknown territory. This single check prevents the // classic runaway across a lawn. if (!arrived && travelled > e->distance * 1.30f) {
stopMotors(); return EDGE_LOST; }
if (arrived) {
stopMotors();
*p = nodePose[currentEdge->toNode]; // <-- RESET. Drift does not
return EDGE_ARRIVED; // accumulate past a node.
driveVW(v, w);
return EDGE_RUNNING;
PROTOCOL — Test protocol — Project 3
- drive a measured 10.00 m straight. Compare odometry to tape
measure. Correct R. Repeat until within 1%. - command ten full 360 degree turns in place. Measure the final
heading error. Correct W. Repeat until within 2 degrees total.
- drive a 4 m square, return to start, WITHOUT any correction - measure the closing error. Typical good result: 100-300 mm. - if it is metres, something is wrong - do not proceed.
- one edge, one termination condition (a wall at the far end) - run 10 times. Does it stop within +/- 100 mm every time? - this proves the reset mechanism works. Everything depends
on it.
- 4-6 nodes. Run 10 times. Log failures BY NODE - failures will cluster at one edge and that edge is your next task.
- place a box, a chair, a person standing still - then have someone walk across the path deliberately - PASS: never touches anything, always recovers or stops safely
- re-verify ToF ranging in direct sun BEFORE running: point at
a wall at 1 m and compare with the indoor reading. Expect degradation; if range collapses, add shrouds or switch that sensor to ultrasonic. - run the route. Log interventions per run.
- 10 consecutive runs without a reset or a human touch - measure battery voltage at the end of each run
PASS CRITERION 8 of 10 full routes with zero human intervention, outdoors, on two different days.
Stage 6’s first line is the one people skip: verify your ranging sensors in sunlight before you trust a route to them.

and checking the reported heading. 3 Build the safety clamp and the hardware e-stop next — before the robot ever drives autonomously. Test the e-stop by
pressing it at full speed. 4 Map your route as a graph on paper. For each edge, write the distance, the heading, and the termination condition. If you

cannot name a termination condition for an edge, redesign the route until you can. 5 Work through stages 2–5 indoors, logging failures by node. 6 Take it outdoors and run stage 6. Report interventions per run and what caused each one — that list is the honest result of
the project.

The PLA problem is real and specific

A 3D-printed PLA bracket that is perfectly rigid in a 24 °C lab will creep and deform inside a dark enclosure standing in direct sun, where internal temperatures of 55–65 °C are ordinary in an Indian summer. Arms droop, motor mounts twist, and your carefully calibrated geometry silently changes.

For anything structural or load-bearing on an outdoor robot, print in PETG or ABS, or use aluminium. Keep PLA for non-structural covers and indoor work. This one material choice prevents a category of failure that is very hard to diagnose, because the part looks fine once it cools down.

topics.title: Mechanical robustness — the unglamorous list

blocks.text: • Every fastener gets thread-lock or a nylon-insert nut. Vibration undoes plain nuts within hours of running. This is the most common single cause of a robot that worked yesterday.
• Strain-relieve every wire where it leaves a moving part or a connector. Wires break at the joint, always. A zip tie 20 mm from the connector, anchored to the chassis, prevents most of it.
• No breadboards and no bare jumper wires on a mobile robot. They work on a desk and disconnect on a paver joint. Solder, or use locking connectors (JST-XH, Molex-style) with proper crimps.
• Label both ends of every cable. When something fails in the field with a crowd watching, you will not have the diagram in your head.
• Loctite or stake the wheel grub screws. A wheel slipping on its shaft looks exactly like an encoder fault and wastes an entire debugging session.

• Design for disassembly. If replacing a motor means removing eleven parts, you will not do it in the field. Aim for any commonly-failing part to be replaceable in under ten minutes with the tools you carry.
• Carry the spares. One motor driver, one motor, one microcontroller, one charged battery, and the crimped cables to fit them.

blocks.text: Never move up two rungs at once. Each stage exists to catch a class of failure cheaply, and a failure caught on the bench costs minutes where the same failure found in front of an audience costs the project.

   exit:       runs 10 min with no reset; current draw as predicted

   catches:    power sag, tuning that only worked unloaded
   exit:       completes the task 5 times; 5 V rail stays above 4.7 V
3 CORRIDOR     real surface, real lighting, longer runs
   catches:    odometry drift, sensor range issues, thermal creep
   exit:       10 minutes continuous, no intervention

catches: clearance, slip, vibration loosening, wheel traction

topics.title: Safety, seriously

blocks.text: These machines are small, but a 4 kg robot at walking pace among people, with pinch points and a lithium battery, deserves the same habits you would apply to something larger. Four non-negotiables:

• The e-stop is hardware. A big, obvious, red, normally-closed switch that breaks the motor supply through a relay or contactor — not a variable your software checks. If the firmware hangs, the e-stop must still work.
• Guard the pinch points. Gears, belts and the arm’s shoulder joint. A cover that costs ten minutes to print prevents a genuinely nasty injury to a curious onlooker.

• Lithium batteries get respect. Charge in a fire-safe bag or on a non-flammable surface, never unattended, never in a hot car, never a pack that is puffed or damaged. Physically secure the pack so it cannot be crushed in a collision.
• Someone is always watching the environment, not the robot. The person with the e-stop should be looking at where the robot is going and who is nearby, while the second person watches the laptop.
Fix Field failure log — one row per event, filled at the time

Time  Stag  What happened  Suspected seam                   Evidence
      e                    (§1.1)                           captured

Fill this in the field, not from memory afterwards. ‘Suspected seam’ forces you to attribute the failure to mechanical, electrical, software or the environment — and after ten rows the pattern is usually unmistakable.

or motor temperature by hand. Record numbers. 4 At stage 6, deliberately have a colleague walk in front of the robot, stand still in its path, and pick it up while running. All

you would design differently. This page is worth more to a future employer than a photograph of the robot.

topics.title: The debugging decision tree

blocks.text: ROBOT IS NOT BEHAVING. Work down this list in order. Do not skip.
1 Is it powered, and does it STAY powered? Meter on the 5 V rail while the motors run. Below 4.7 V -> power problem, not a software problem. Stop here and fix it. (2.7)
2 Does it do the same wrong thing every time?
REPEATABLE -> logic, calibration or wiring. Tractable.
RANDOM -> power, ground, connector, or a loose fastener.
Wiggle every connector with the robot running.

3 Did it work before? What changed? Code, a battery swap, a part replaced, the surface, the temperature, the time of day, someone else touching it. Something changed. Find the change before forming a theory.
4 Are the SENSORS telling the truth? Print raw values and move the robot by hand. Do not debug a control loop that is being fed nonsense. Half of all "PID won't tune" problems are sensor problems.
5 Are the ACTUATORS doing what you commanded? Command a fixed output with the loop disabled. Does the wheel turn at the expected speed, in the expected direction?
6 Is the LOOP RATE what you think? Print the actual interval. Jitter or a slow loop invalidates every gain you tuned. (3.3)
7 Is anything SATURATING? Log the pre-clamp controller output. If it is pinned at the limit, no amount of tuning helps - you have an actuator sizing problem.
8 ONLY NOW look at the control algorithm.
"What changed?" and "What is it actually measuring?"
Steps 1–3 resolve the majority of field failures and take about five minutes

On the LiDAR question in §6.1. Entry-level 2D LiDAR prices have fallen sharply, driven largely by the robot-vacuum market, and units around ₹5,000–₹9,000 are now readily available including in India. The argument in this guide is not that you cannot afford one — it is that entry units are typically specified for indoor ambient light of roughly 2 klux while direct sunlight exceeds 100 klux, that sunlight-capable units cost several times more, and that metric SLAM is the wrong architecture for fixed campus routes anyway. If your bot runs indoors, revisit that decision: cheap LiDAR plus a Linux board is a perfectly good architecture there. Check current prices and lux ratings before you choose.

And the sentence to take away. Robustness is not the boring cousin of sophistication — it is the harder engineering problem. Anyone can make a robot work once, in a lab, with the person who built it standing next to it. Making it work ten times out of ten, outdoors, in the heat, with a stranger operating it, requires you to have thought about the power rail, the connectors, the calibration procedure, the failure states and the people. That is the whole discipline, and the parts of it that look unglamorous are the parts that decide whether the thing exists.
